=== migration ===
-- DevsAssemble — 0001 profiles
-- Identity foundation: profile per auth user, role-based access, RLS.
-- Apply to a DEDICATED DevsAssemble Supabase project (see build plan).

create extension if not exists citext;

-- Roles are the single source of truth for authorization (used by RLS + DAL).
create type public.user_role as enum ('member', 'moderator', 'admin');

create table public.profiles (
  id            uuid primary key references auth.users (id) on delete cascade,
  username      citext unique not null,
  display_name  text,
  avatar_url    text,
  bio           text,
  github_username text,
  github_user_id  bigint,
  website_url   text,
  x_url         text,
  linkedin_url  text,
  role          public.user_role not null default 'member',
  is_banned     boolean not null default false,
  created_at    timestamptz not null default now(),
  updated_at    timestamptz not null default now()
);

comment on table public.profiles is 'Public member profile, 1:1 with auth.users.';

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- updated_at maintenance
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
create or replace function public.set_updated_at()
returns trigger
language plpgsql
as $$
begin
  new.updated_at = now();
  return new;
end;
$$;

create trigger profiles_set_updated_at
  before update on public.profiles
  for each row execute function public.set_updated_at();

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Seed a profile whenever a new auth user is created. Pulls GitHub metadata
-- from the OAuth identity payload; falls back to an email-derived username.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
create or replace function public.handle_new_user()
returns trigger
language plpgsql
security definer
set search_path = public
as $$
declare
  meta jsonb := new.raw_user_meta_data;
  base_username text;
  final_username text;
  suffix int := 0;
begin
  base_username := coalesce(
    meta ->> 'user_name',            -- GitHub login
    meta ->> 'preferred_username',
    split_part(new.email, '@', 1),
    'member'
  );
  base_username := lower(regexp_replace(base_username, '[^a-zA-Z0-9_]', '', 'g'));
  if base_username = '' then
    base_username := 'member';
  end if;

  final_username := base_username;
  while exists (select 1 from public.profiles where username = final_username) loop
    suffix := suffix + 1;
    final_username := base_username || suffix::text;
  end loop;

  insert into public.profiles (id, username, display_name, avatar_url, github_username, github_user_id)
  values (
    new.id,
    final_username,
    coalesce(meta ->> 'full_name', meta ->> 'name', final_username),
    meta ->> 'avatar_url',
    meta ->> 'user_name',
    nullif(meta ->> 'provider_id', '')::bigint
  );
  return new;
end;
$$;

create trigger on_auth_user_created
  after insert on auth.users
  for each row execute function public.handle_new_user();

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Authorization helpers (SECURITY DEFINER, locked search_path).
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
create or replace function public.current_user_role()
returns public.user_role
language sql
stable
security definer
set search_path = public
as $$
  select role from public.profiles where id = auth.uid();
$$;

create or replace function public.is_admin()
returns boolean
language sql
stable
security definer
set search_path = public
as $$
  select public.current_user_role() in ('admin', 'moderator');
$$;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Prevent privilege escalation: only admins may change role/is_banned.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
create or replace function public.guard_profile_privileges()
returns trigger
language plpgsql
security definer
set search_path = public
as $$
begin
  if (new.role is distinct from old.role
      or new.is_banned is distinct from old.is_banned)
     and not public.is_admin() then
    raise exception 'Not authorized to change role or ban status';
  end if;
  return new;
end;
$$;

create trigger profiles_guard_privileges
  before update on public.profiles
  for each row execute function public.guard_profile_privileges();

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Row Level Security
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
alter table public.profiles enable row level security;

-- Public read: profiles are public pages.
create policy "profiles_select_public"
  on public.profiles for select
  using (true);

-- Self-update only (role/is_banned still gated by the trigger above).
create policy "profiles_update_self"
  on public.profiles for update
  to authenticated
  using (id = auth.uid())
  with check (id = auth.uid());

-- Admins can update any profile (roles, bans, moderation).
create policy "profiles_update_admin"
  on public.profiles for update
  to authenticated
  using (public.is_admin())
  with check (public.is_admin());

-- Note: INSERT happens only via the handle_new_user trigger (security definer),
-- so no INSERT policy is granted to clients.

Good — now I have the real picture. DevsAssemble isn't a generic forum: it's a **branded dev community** (comic/superhero identity, custom logo/buttons) on Next.js 16 + Supabase, with GitHub OAuth, role-based profiles + RLS moderation already built, and — per your own notes — **events/RSVP, likes, comments, and posting** as the interaction model. That last part matters a lot for this decision.

Here's my assessment.

## The core tension

Discourse is a *forum engine*. It's exceptional at threaded discussion, trust levels, moderation, search, email digests, and spam control — years of hard-won maturity you'd otherwise reinvent. But it is opinionated Rails software with its own data model, its own admin, its own theming system (Ember + SCSS), and its own hosting story (Docker, Postgres, Redis, Sidekiq, a mail server).

Your product, based on what's in the repo, is **not primarily a forum**. It's an events-and-people community with a strong custom brand. Discourse can *do* discussion inside that, but it can't be the shell — and bending it into an events-first, comic-branded product is where the "just use Discourse" promise quietly falls apart.

## What each path actually costs you

**Build from scratch (continue current stack)**
- You already have the hardest security foundation done well: RLS, role enum, privilege-escalation guards, OAuth profile seeding. That's real work that's already banked.
- You own the data model, the brand, and the interaction design completely — events/RSVP are first-class instead of bolted on.
- The cost is everything Discourse gives for free: spam/abuse defenses, notification/email infrastructure, full-text search, rich text editing, flagging/moderation queues, trust levels, rate limiting. Each is a real project. **Rich text + spam + email notifications** are the three that consistently eat far more time than teams expect.

**Adopt Discourse**
- Instant, battle-tested discussion + moderation + email + search on day one.
- But: separate hosting/ops (or ~$100+/mo managed), a second auth story to reconcile with your Supabase/GitHub identity (SSO bridge — doable but real), a second data store that your events/profiles must integrate with via API, and theming that will fight your comic brand. You'd effectively run *two* apps and stitch them.
- You'd likely be discarding the profiles/RLS work you've already shipped, since Discourse owns users.

## My recommendation

**Keep building your own shell; don't adopt Discourse as the platform.** Your product's center of gravity (events, RSVP, branded identity, GitHub-native profiles) is not what Discourse optimizes for, and integrating it would mean running two systems and reconciling two identity models — more total complexity than it removes.

**But steal Discourse's lessons, and don't rebuild its hardest parts from scratch:**
- **Discussion/comments** — this is the one area where, *if* long threaded discussion becomes central, embedding Discourse (via its SSO + `<iframe>`/API, or Discourse as a headless comment backend) is worth reconsidering. If comments stay lightweight (event chatter, post replies), build them on Supabase.
- **Email/notifications** — use a Marketplace email provider (Resend/Postmark) rather than running a mail server. This is the single biggest thing Discourse gives you that you shouldn't hand-roll.
- **Spam/abuse** — lean on GitHub-OAuth-only signup (you already do) as your first line; it eliminates most drive-by spam that Discourse has to fight because it allows email signups.
- **Full-text search** — Postgres `tsvector` (native in Supabase) covers you until scale demands otherwise.

**When I'd flip the recommendation:** if within 6 months the product becomes primarily long-form threaded discussion (a Q&A/forum destination) rather than events + profiles, Discourse's maturity would outweigh the integration tax. Nothing you've built so far locks you out of that — profiles and events can coexist with an embedded Discourse later.

Want me to sketch the Supabase schema for the events/RSVP/comments/likes layer, or spike what a Discourse-SSO integration would actually require so you can see the real cost before deciding?

I just want to make sure I'm not going to regret not starting with Discourse. To be clear, I don't like using big bulky 3P software.  This can be small, and focused on what we care about with a custom solution.

Then you're aligned with the grain of what you've already built, and I don't think you'll regret it. Let me give you the honest version rather than just telling you what you want to hear.

**Why skipping Discourse is the right call for you specifically:**

- **The "regret" scenario for going custom is rebuilding moderation and spam control at 3am when a community turns on you.** You've already pre-empted the biggest one: GitHub-OAuth-only signup kills ~90% of the spam that Discourse exists to fight. Discourse carries all that machinery because it must support open email signup. You don't. That's the single fact that most changes the math in your favor.

- **The other classic regret is "we outgrew our hand-rolled forum."** But you're not building a forum. Discourse's depth (trust levels, threaded reply trees, digests, a plugin ecosystem) is depth in a direction you don't primarily care about. Adopting it means paying for a whole discussion engine to get the 20% you'd use — and then fighting it to make events and your comic brand first-class. That's the actual bulk you don't want.

- **Small and focused is a legitimate, durable architecture here — not a shortcut you pay for later.** Postgres full-text search, Supabase RLS, and a Resend/Postmark for email cover the genuinely hard parts without a second system, a second identity model, or a Docker/Redis/Sidekiq stack to babysit. You keep one app, one data store, one deploy.

**The one thing to be honest with yourself about** — the *only* place I'd say "measure twice": if this ever pivots to being **primarily** a long-form discussion destination (a Stack-Overflow-ish Q&A or a deep forum where threads are the product), Discourse's maturity would genuinely outclass a custom build. The good news is nothing you've built forecloses that — profiles and events sit happily alongside an embedded Discourse if that day comes. So it's not a door you're closing now; it's a decision you can defer until the product actually asks for it.

Net: your instinct is sound. Build small, own your data model, and don't run someone else's Rails monolith to get comment threads. The only discipline required is to **not accidentally rebuild Discourse** — keep the discussion layer deliberately lightweight, and buy (don't build) email delivery.

Want me to lay out the minimal schema for the interaction layer (events/RSVP/posts/comments/likes) so "small and focused" has a concrete shape to hold you to?

I do think that there's a possibility we run a forum of sorts.  A place for people to start discussion topics and have a conversation that includes the ability to share images, videos, gifs, text, and link previews.

This is the detail that actually deserves a second look, so let me be straight with you rather than just staying consistent with what I said before.

What you're describing — topics, conversations, images/video/gifs, link previews — is a **real forum**, not the lightweight comment layer I was picturing. That does move the needle. But here's the honest calculus: it moves you toward "be disciplined," not toward "you need Discourse."

**Why it's still a sound custom build:**

The thing that makes Discourse worth its bulk isn't the features you listed — it's the *operational* forum problems: open-signup spam, moderation queues, trust systems, email deliverability at scale. GitHub-only auth already defuses the worst of those. The features you named are, individually, solved problems you *assemble* rather than *invent*.

**The key distinction — "custom" should not mean "from scratch" for these:**

| Piece | Don't hand-roll | Do this instead |
|---|---|---|
| Rich text editing | The editor itself | Adopt **Tiptap** or **Lexical** — this is a multi-month trap if you build it |
| Image/video/gif upload | Storage + resize pipeline | **Supabase Storage** or **Vercel Blob**, direct client upload (function bodies cap at 4.5MB, so you *must* upload direct-to-blob anyway) |
| Link previews | The fetch-and-parse | OG-tag fetcher + cache — but **guard against SSRF** (you're fetching arbitrary user URLs server-side; this is a real vuln, not a nicety) |
| Search | | Postgres `tsvector`, native in Supabase |
| Rendering user content | | **Sanitize aggressively** — rich media + user HTML is the #1 XSS surface; get this wrong once and it's the actual 3am incident |

**The parts that are genuinely more work now than a comment layer** — and where the "we should've used Discourse" regret could actually come from if you underinvest:

1. **Content moderation of media.** Text you can ban a user over. Images/video/gifs mean someone *will* post something illegal or abusive, and you need a flagging + takedown + review flow. Discourse ships this. You'd build it.
2. **Notifications** (replied-to-you, @mentions, "watching this topic") + email digests. This is the feature users quietly expect from a forum and it's more plumbing than it looks.
3. **XSS/SSRF security surface**, per the table — rich media raises the stakes on getting sanitization and URL-fetching right.

**My verdict, updated:** still build it, still custom, still small-ish — but go in knowing a rich-media forum is a **bigger commitment than a discussion sidecar**, and that the real cost is moderation + notifications + content security, not the topic/reply data model. If you're willing to fund those three deliberately, you'll get something focused and yours that Discourse could never brand or shape the way you want. If those three feel like more than you want to own, *that's* your actual signal to embed Discourse for the forum specifically — not the media features.

One concrete way to de-risk the decision: I can sketch the schema + the moderation/notification surface for the forum layer so the full scope is visible on one page. Seeing it laid out is usually what makes "build vs. embed" obvious. Want that?

# DevsAssemble — Build Plan

_Last updated: 2026-09-28_

Living plan for DevsAssemble: a branded developer community (comic/superhero
identity) built on Next.js 16 + Supabase. This document captures the major
architectural decisions, the forum scope, and the risks we're choosing to own.

---

## Guiding principles

- **Small, focused, and ours.** No bulky third-party platform we have to bend to
  our brand. One app, one data store, one deploy.
- **Public read, auth to interact.** All content is publicly readable; only
  likes, comments, RSVP, and posting require sign-in.
- **GitHub-OAuth-only signup.** This is a load-bearing decision, not a
  convenience — it removes ~90% of the drive-by spam a forum otherwise fights.
- **Assemble, don't invent.** "Custom" means we own the data model and product
  shape. It does *not* mean hand-rolling solved infrastructure (rich text
  editors, blob storage, email delivery).

---

## Decision: build custom vs. adopt Discourse

**Decision: build custom. Do not adopt Discourse as the platform.**

### Why

- DevsAssemble's center of gravity is **events + people + brand**, not threaded
  discussion. Discourse optimizes for the forum; making events and our comic
  brand first-class inside it means fighting the tool.
- Adopting Discourse means running **two systems** (separate Rails/Docker/Redis/
  Sidekiq stack), reconciling **two identity models** (Discourse users vs. our
  Supabase/GitHub profiles + RLS), and discarding the profiles/RLS/moderation
  foundation already shipped.
- The operational problems that justify Discourse's bulk — open-signup spam,
  email deliverability at scale, trust systems — are largely defused for us by
  **GitHub-only auth** and a managed email provider.

### The forum is in scope

We do intend to run a forum: users start discussion **topics** and have
**conversations** that support **text, images, video, GIFs, and link previews**.
This is a *real forum*, not a lightweight comment sidecar. It raises the
commitment — but it moves us toward "be disciplined," not toward "adopt
Discourse."

### When we would revisit this

If DevsAssemble ever becomes **primarily** a long-form discussion / Q&A
destination (threads *are* the product), Discourse's maturity would outclass a
custom build. Nothing we build forecloses this — profiles and events can coexist
with an **embedded Discourse** (SSO bridge) added later for the forum only. It's
a deferrable decision, not a closing door.

---

## Architecture: assemble, don't hand-roll

For the forum + rich-media layer, buy/adopt the hard infrastructure; build the
product model.

| Concern | Do NOT hand-roll | Approach |
|---|---|---|
| Rich text editing | The editor engine | Adopt **Tiptap** or **Lexical**. Hand-rolling this is a multi-month trap. |
| Image / video / GIF upload | Storage + resize pipeline | **Supabase Storage** or **Vercel Blob**, **direct client upload** (Vercel function bodies cap at 4.5 MB, so direct-to-blob is required regardless). |
| Link previews | The fetch-and-parse | Server-side OG-tag fetcher + cache. **Must guard against SSRF** — we fetch arbitrary user-supplied URLs server-side. |
| Search | A search service (for now) | Postgres `tsvector`, native in Supabase. Revisit only if scale demands. |
| Email / notifications | A mail server | Marketplace email provider (**Resend** / **Postmark**). |
| Rendering user content | | **Sanitize aggressively.** Rich media + user HTML is the #1 XSS surface. |

---

## Risks we are deliberately choosing to own

These are the three areas where "we should have used Discourse" regret could
actually originate if we underinvest. Fund them intentionally.

1. **Content moderation of media.** Someone *will* post something illegal or
   abusive. We need flagging → takedown → review, not just user bans. Discourse
   ships this; we build it.
2. **Notifications + email digests.** replied-to-you, @mentions, "watching this
   topic." Quietly expected of any forum; more plumbing than it looks.
3. **Content security (XSS / SSRF).** Rich media raises the stakes on
   sanitization and server-side URL fetching. Getting this wrong once is the
   real 3am incident.

---

## Current foundation (shipped)

- Supabase project with `profiles` table (1:1 with `auth.users`).
- Role enum (`member` / `moderator` / `admin`), RLS, privilege-escalation guard,
  ban flag.
- GitHub OAuth with profile auto-seeding from OAuth metadata.
- App shell: dashboard, login, settings/profile. Comic brand components.

---

## Forum work breakdown (tracked as GitHub issues)

See the `forum` label in
[jeffblankenburg/devsassemble issues](https://github.com/jeffblankenburg/devsassemble/issues).

1. **Schema** — categories, topics, posts (threaded replies), reactions/likes.
2. **Rich text editor** — Tiptap/Lexical integration, serialization format.
3. **Media uploads** — direct-to-blob, validation, thumbnails.
4. **Link previews** — OG fetcher + cache, SSRF guard.
5. **Rendering + sanitization** — XSS-safe render of stored content.
6. **Moderation** — flagging, review queue, takedown, audit trail.
7. **Notifications** — in-app + email (Resend/Postmark), @mentions, watching.
8. **Search** — Postgres full-text over topics/posts.

content.text:
Done. Everything's captured in both the plan and issues.

## What's now in place

**`docs/PLAN.md`** — versioned in the repo, covering:
- The build-vs-Discourse decision + rationale, and the explicit condition under which we'd revisit it
- Forum scope (rich media: text, images, video, GIFs, link previews)
- The "assemble, don't hand-roll" architecture table
- The three deliberately-owned risks (media moderation, notifications, XSS/SSRF)
- The new **agent-destination** direction
- A full epic→issue map

**26 GitHub issues** under 8 epics:

| # | Epic | Children |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Platform foundation & infra | — |
| 2 | Events & RSVP | #14, #15 |
| 3 | Community feed | #16 |
| 4 | Forum (rich-media) | #9–#13 |
| 5 | **Agent destination & evaluations** | #20–#26 |
| 6 | Moderation, trust & safety | #17 |
| 7 | Notifications & email | #18 |
| 8 | Search & discovery | #19 |

## On the agent-destination idea (since you wanted to investigate it)

This is the most differentiating thing in the whole plan, and I structured issue #5 around a specific thesis worth your reaction:

**The unlock isn't "add an API" — it's that authoritativeness for agents is a *trust* problem, not a *format* problem.** Any site can emit JSON. What makes DevsAssemble worth an agent querying is that the underlying evaluations are *hard to fake* — and your existing GitHub-only auth + profiles/RLS foundation is already the beginning of that moat. That's why #26 (provenance & anti-gaming) sits in the agent epic, not the moderation one: for agents, the provenance *is* the product.

Two things I'd flag for you to weigh before we build here:
- **Aggregation needs to expose the "why," not just a score** (#21). An agent asking "should this developer use X" needs distribution + rationale, or it's just a star rating it could get anywhere.
- **MCP vs. plain API** (#22 vs #23) — I filed both, but they're somewhat competing bets on how agents will actually reach you. Worth deciding which is the primary surface rather than half-building both.

Want me to spike the entity + evaluation schema (#20) next, since it's the foundation the whole agent layer stands on?
If I wanted to launch an MVP tomorrow, what features should I include to start?

Here's the honest "tomorrow" cut. The constraint isn't taste — it's that a rich-media forum, moderation queues, notifications, and an agent API cannot be built in a day. So MVP = **leverage what's already shipped + add exactly one content loop + keep one safety net.**

## Ship it

**Already done (your MVP is half-built):**
- GitHub OAuth, profiles, roles/RLS, ban flag, app shell. This is the expensive, security-sensitive part — and it's banked.

**Add tomorrow — one content loop only:**
- **Text discussion: topics + threaded replies.** Markdown, no media uploads, no link unfurl, no rich-text editor. This is a thin layer on the Supabase/RLS pattern you already have (issue #9, stripped down).
- **Likes** on posts (trivial join table, public-read).
- **Public profile pages** — you have the data; just render it. Gives people an identity to show up for.

**The one non-negotiable safety net:**
- **Report button + admin delete.** You already have `moderator`/`admin` roles and the ban flag — wire a minimal "flag → admins see it → delete/ban" path. Public UGC with *no* takedown ability is a real liability on day one, even at ten users. This is the minimum viable slice of issue #17, not the full queue.

## Explicitly cut (and why it's safe)

| Deferred | Why it waits |
|---|---|
| Media uploads, GIFs, video | The XSS/SSRF/moderation surface (#12–#14) is exactly what you can't rush. Markdown-only sidesteps all of it. |
| Link previews | Same — SSRF guard is not a same-day job. Links still work as plain links. |
| Rich text editor | A `<textarea>` + markdown render ships tomorrow; Tiptap/Lexical is a real integration. |
| Email notifications | No provider wiring day one. In-app "unread" can come week two. |
| Events & RSVP | A brand-new community has no one to attend events yet — chicken-and-egg. Add once there are members. |
| Agent API / MCP / evaluations | **The whole agent vision needs content to exist first.** You can't aggregate developer temperament from an empty forum. This is a phase-2 payoff, not a launch feature. |
| Full-text search | Not needed at low volume; browse + recency ordering is fine. |

## The one fork worth a beat

I'm recommending **discussion as the core loop** over events because it (a) is the cheapest same-day build, and (b) generates exactly the sentiment/discussion data your agent-and-evaluations vision later feeds on. If your actual launch plan is "I have a specific event to gather people around," then events-first flips that — but for a cold start, discussion is the better seed.

One thing to protect even in MVP: **don't let markdown rendering become an XSS hole.** Even text-only, sanitize the rendered output. It's the single security corner you can't cut, and it's small.

Want me to spec the stripped-down MVP as its own tracked issue (or a `mvp` milestone across #9/#16/#17) so tomorrow's build has a clean checklist?
Events are the carrot that we dangle to get people to want to join.  Can't cut events.

Agreed — and that actually makes the MVP *tighter*, not bigger, because it changes what the core loop is. Events aren't just a feature here; **RSVP is your signup funnel.** Public browse → "I want in" → sign in with GitHub to RSVP → now they're a member. That maps exactly to your "public read, auth to interact" model, and it means events do double duty as both the carrot and the conversion mechanism.

Here's the revised tomorrow cut.

## Ship it — events as the core loop

**Already done:** GitHub OAuth, profiles, roles/RLS, ban flag, app shell.

**Add tomorrow:**
- **Public event listing + event detail pages** — browsable with no auth. This is the carrot; it has to look good and be fully public (lean on your comic brand here).
- **RSVP (going / interested)** — auth-gated. This *is* the sign-up moment. First RSVP = GitHub sign-in = new member.
- **"Who's going" on each event** — render RSVP'd profiles. Social proof is itself a draw, and it gives your existing profile pages a reason to exist on day one.
- **Admin-created events only.** You and mods seed events; members can't create them yet. This is the single biggest scope cut — it removes the event-authoring UI, permissions, and validation, and for a cold launch you *want* to curate the first events anyway.

## The safety-net math just got easier

With events admin-created and **RSVP as the only user write**, there's almost no user-generated content to moderate at launch — your existing ban flag covers it. That's a real gift: you can skip the report/delete queue entirely *if* you also hold back free-text.

The catch: the moment you add **event comments/discussion**, you reintroduce the moderation surface. So for literal-tomorrow, I'd cut event comments too and keep launch to browse + RSVP.

## Sequencing (the honest part)

You can't build events *and* discussion well in one day. So:

1. **Tomorrow:** events + RSVP + profiles. Proves the carrot converts.
2. **Fast-follow (days, not weeks):** discussion — text-only topics/replies + report/delete. This is what turns one-time RSVPers into a *returning* community and starts feeding the evaluation/agent data flywheel. It's issue #9 stripped down; it's ready to go the moment events are live.

Events get people in the door once. Discussion is what makes them come back. Ship the door first — but have #9 queued so the gap between "attended one event" and "there's nothing to do here" is measured in days.

Want me to reframe issues #2/#14/#15 into a concrete `mvp` milestone (admin-created events + RSVP + who's-going, comments explicitly out) so tomorrow's build has a clean checklist, and tag #9 as the fast-follow?
sure

1	# DevsAssemble — Build Plan
2	
3	_Last updated: 2026-09-28_
4	
5	Living plan for DevsAssemble: a branded developer community (comic/superhero
6	identity) built on Next.js 16 + Supabase. This document captures the major
7	architectural decisions, the forum scope, and the risks we're choosing to own.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## Guiding principles
12	
13	- **Small, focused, and ours.** No bulky third-party platform we have to bend to
14	  our brand. One app, one data store, one deploy.
15	- **Public read, auth to interact.** All content is publicly readable; only
16	  likes, comments, RSVP, and posting require sign-in.
17	- **GitHub-OAuth-only signup.** This is a load-bearing decision, not a
18	  convenience — it removes ~90% of the drive-by spam a forum otherwise fights.
19	- **Assemble, don't invent.** "Custom" means we own the data model and product
20	  shape. It does *not* mean hand-rolling solved infrastructure (rich text
21	  editors, blob storage, email delivery).
22	
23	---
24	
25	## Decision: build custom vs. adopt Discourse
26	
27	**Decision: build custom. Do not adopt Discourse as the platform.**
28	
29	### Why
30	
31	- DevsAssemble's center of gravity is **events + people + brand**, not threaded
32	  discussion. Discourse optimizes for the forum; making events and our comic
33	  brand first-class inside it means fighting the tool.
34	- Adopting Discourse means running **two systems** (separate Rails/Docker/Redis/
35	  Sidekiq stack), reconciling **two identity models** (Discourse users vs. our
36	  Supabase/GitHub profiles + RLS), and discarding the profiles/RLS/moderation
37	  foundation already shipped.
38	- The operational problems that justify Discourse's bulk — open-signup spam,
39	  email deliverability at scale, trust systems — are largely defused for us by
40	  **GitHub-only auth** and a managed email provider.
41	
42	### The forum is in scope
43	
44	We do intend to run a forum: users start discussion **topics** and have
45	**conversations** that support **text, images, video, GIFs, and link previews**.
46	This is a *real forum*, not a lightweight comment sidecar. It raises the
47	commitment — but it moves us toward "be disciplined," not toward "adopt
48	Discourse."
49	
50	### Forum non-negotiables
51	
52	Two requirements are treated as necessities, not enhancements — they are the
53	difference between a forum and a chat log, and they underpin the agent-destination
54	goal (agents and search engines can only cite what is stable and findable):
55	
56	- **Truly searchable threads.** Full-text search across all topics and posts is a
57	  launch requirement for the forum, not a later nicety. See [#19](https://github.com/jeffblankenburg/devsassemble/issues/19).
58	- **Permanent URLs.** Every topic and post has a stable, canonical, never-changing
59	  URL that survives title edits, renames, and moves (id-based, slug is cosmetic).
60	  Old URLs must never 404 or silently repoint. This makes threads linkable,
61	  bookmarkable, crawlable, and citable — by humans and agents alike.
62	
63	### When we would revisit this
64	
65	If DevsAssemble ever becomes **primarily** a long-form discussion / Q&A
66	destination (threads *are* the product), Discourse's maturity would outclass a
67	custom build. Nothing we build forecloses this — profiles and events can coexist
68	with an **embedded Discourse** (SSO bridge) added later for the forum only. It's
69	a deferrable decision, not a closing door.
70	
71	---
72	
73	## Architecture: assemble, don't hand-roll
74	
75	For the forum + rich-media layer, buy/adopt the hard infrastructure; build the
76	product model.
77	
78	| Concern | Do NOT hand-roll | Approach |
79	|---|---|---|
80	| Rich text editing | The editor engine | Adopt **Tiptap** or **Lexical**. Hand-rolling this is a multi-month trap. |
81	| Image / video / GIF upload | Storage + resize pipeline | **Supabase Storage** or **Vercel Blob**, **direct client upload** (Vercel function bodies cap at 4.5 MB, so direct-to-blob is required regardless). |
82	| Link previews | The fetch-and-parse | Server-side OG-tag fetcher + cache. **Must guard against SSRF** — we fetch arbitrary user-supplied URLs server-side. |
83	| Search | A search service (for now) | Postgres `tsvector`, native in Supabase. Revisit only if scale demands. |
84	| Email / notifications | A mail server | Marketplace email provider (**Resend** / **Postmark**). |
85	| Rendering user content | | **Sanitize aggressively.** Rich media + user HTML is the #1 XSS surface. |
86	
87	---
88	
89	## Risks we are deliberately choosing to own
90	
91	These are the three areas where "we should have used Discourse" regret could
92	actually originate if we underinvest. Fund them intentionally.
93	
94	1. **Content moderation of media.** Someone *will* post something illegal or
95	   abusive. We need flagging → takedown → review, not just user bans. Discourse
96	   ships this; we build it.
97	2. **Notifications + email digests.** replied-to-you, @mentions, "watching this
98	   topic." Quietly expected of any forum; more plumbing than it looks.
99	3. **Content security (XSS / SSRF).** Rich media raises the stakes on
100	   sanitization and server-side URL fetching. Getting this wrong once is the
101	   real 3am incident.
102	
103	---
104	
105	## Direction: a destination for agents, not just AI builders
106	
107	DevsAssemble should be authoritative for AI *agents*, not only human AI
108	*builders* — a machine-readable place where agents can evaluate **developer
109	temperament toward tools, resources, and practices**.
110	
111	- **The data:** developers rate and review tools/resources with structured
112	  sentiment + rationale. Aggregated into "developer temperament" signals (score +
113	  distribution + the *why*, not a single number).
114	- **The access:** first-class agent surfaces — a public read JSON API, an **MCP
115	  server**, `llms.txt` + schema.org structured data for discoverability, and
116	  agent auth + rate limiting for controlled programmatic access.
117	- **The trust:** authoritativeness depends on provenance. GitHub-only auth is the
118	  first line of defense; evaluations carry author-trust signals so agents can
119	  weight them and we can resist brigading/sockpuppets. Ties into moderation.
120	- **The flywheel:** the same human activity (forum sentiment, reviews, feed
121	  discussion) feeds the machine-readable evaluation layer.
122	
123	Tracked under the `agent` and `evaluations` labels.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Restream's embed player for websites:

## Overview
The Website Video Player allows you to stream directly on your website and reach your viewers and clients at the best place - your home page.

## How to Set Up

From your home screen, click the Channels button, click Add New, and select Embed Player. Choose a display name for your reference only to make it easier to recognize in your channels list. Once the channel is added, your unique iframe embed code will appear.

## Configuration Options

You can choose between a responsive or fixed-size player and enable or disable the viewer counter. Once added, the embed player will show an "Offline" state until the stream goes live.

## Using the Embed Code

Paste it into the HTML of the website page where you want the stream to appear. The player integrates perfectly with WordPress, Magento, Ghost, Shopify, Squarespace, GoDaddy, and Wix.

For detailed setup instructions, you can visit the official Restream support page at https://support.restream.io/en/articles/4996608-stream-to-your-website.

content.text:
Verified — and the news is good. This is an easy integration, and it fits your existing stack cleanly.

## The player itself: trivial

Restream has a dedicated **Embed Player** channel type. You add it as a "channel" in Restream, and it hands you an **iframe embed code**. Drop that iframe on your home page and you're done. Two things that matter for your use case:

- It **self-manages state** — shows an "Offline" placeholder until you go live, then auto-plays the broadcast. So the naive version ("always embed it") already mostly does what you want with zero backend.
- Responsive or fixed size, optional viewer counter.

That's the whole "play it on the page" story. It's an iframe.

## The real question: "when we're live"

You have two tiers, and for launch I'd go with the simpler one:

**MVP — manual toggle (recommended, zero Restream API work):**
- A `live` flag in Supabase (tie it to the event that's being broadcast — this connects to your events epic).
- One admin click when the meeting starts flips the flag.
- Home page subscribes via **Supabase Realtime** → the "🔴 LIVE NOW" hero + iframe appears instantly for everyone, no refresh.
- The iframe's own offline state is your safety net if someone forgets to toggle.

This needs *nothing* from Restream beyond the embed code, and it's maybe an afternoon on your current stack.

**Later — auto-detect:** Restream exposes a **WebSocket "Streaming Updates" API** (`wss://streaming.api.restream.io/ws`, OAuth) that emits `CONNECTED`/`DISCONNECTED` events + viewer counts. You could have that flip the flag automatically so there's no manual step. It's more work (a persistent connection doesn't fit serverless neatly — you'd need a small worker or a poll), so it's a nice-to-have, not launch-critical.

## Two caveats worth checking now

1. **Plan tier** — the website/embed player is a **paid Restream feature**. Confirm your plan includes it before you build around it.
2. **CSP** — embedding a third-party iframe means adding Restream to your `frame-src` content-security-policy. Minor, but do it deliberately rather than loosening CSP broadly.

Net: yes, easy. The iframe is the easy 90%; the "reveal when live" is a small Supabase flag + Realtime, not a heavy integration.

Want me to file this as an issue (home-page live broadcast — embed player + `live` flag + Realtime, tied to the events epic), and note the auto-detect WebSocket path as a fast-follow?

Sources: [Restream — stream to your website](https://support.restream.io/en/articles/4996608-stream-to-your-website), [Restream web player](https://restream.io/web-player), [Restream Streaming Updates API](https://developers.restream.io/private-api/streaming-updates)

# Build decisions & review notes

Running log of judgment calls made while building autonomously, and — more
importantly — **what needs your eyes**. Newest sections at the bottom.

Legend: 🔴 needs your verification · 🟡 a simplification to revisit · 🟢 FYI

---

## Git topology

- 🟢 The entire pre-existing app was **uncommitted** (untracked on `main`). I
  committed it as a baseline (`build/baseline`, PR #37) so each feature chunk has
  a clean diff.
- 🟢 Feature branches are **stacked on `build/baseline`**; their PRs target
  `build/baseline`. **Merge order:** merge #37 first, then retarget/merge each
  feature PR to `main`. GitHub will show clean diffs once the base is merged.
- 🟢 I never push `main` and never deploy — per your guardrails.
- 🟡 `.env.example` is covered by `.gitignore` (`.env*`), so it is NOT committed.
  You may want to force-add it (`git add -f .env.example`) as a template for new
  contributors. I did not override your ignore rule.

## Events chunk (branch `build/events`)

- 🔴 **RSVP sign-up funnel** — I threaded a `next` destination through GitHub
  OAuth *and* email OTP so an RSVP while logged out returns to the event after
  sign-in (`?next=/events/<slug>`). I **cannot test the OAuth round trip
  headless** — please verify: logged-out → click "RSVP — sign in to join" →
  GitHub → land back on the event page, then RSVP completes. This is the funnel
  you flagged as the #1 risk.
- 🟢 Open-redirect hardening: `lib/auth/redirects.ts#safeNext` restricts `next`
  to same-origin absolute paths; applied in the login page, both auth actions,
  and the callback + confirm routes.
- 🟡 **Event time handling** — times are stored as the admin's wall-clock
  interpreted as **UTC** and always displayed in **UTC** with a timezone *label*
  (e.g. "1:00 PM ET"). So the displayed time equals exactly what was entered.
  This is predictable and bug-free for a single-community listing, but is NOT
  true multi-timezone handling. Revisit with a TZ library if events ever span
  zones. See `lib/events/format.ts`.
- 🟢 **Admin-only event authoring** at launch (per the MVP decision): members
  cannot create events; RLS gates writes to `is_admin()`. Admin UI at
  `/admin/events`.
- 🟡 **Dynamic route pages use inline param types** (`{ params: Promise<{ slug:
  string }> }`) instead of the repo's `PageProps<"/route">` convention, because
  Next's generated route types (`.next/types`) can't be regenerated in my
  environment (that needs `next dev`/`next build`, which are yours). Once you run
  the app, you may switch these two files back to `PageProps<...>` if you prefer
  the convention: `app/events/[slug]/page.tsx`,
  `app/(app)/admin/events/[id]/edit/page.tsx`.
- 🟢 **Verification ceiling:** `tsc --noEmit` and `eslint` both pass. I did not
  run `next build` (it shares `.next` with your dev server) or exercise the UI in
  a browser. Treat runtime/visual behavior as unverified pending your pass.
- 🟢 **Seed data:** I inserted 3 sample **published** events directly in Supabase
  so `/events` and the (soon) wired home page render real content for your review.
  Delete them anytime via `/admin/events`. They have `created_by = null`.
- 🟢 **Live broadcast groundwork:** the event detail page renders a Restream
  `<iframe>` when `is_live` + `stream_embed_url` are set (full home-page live flow
  is issue #35). Needs your Restream plan + embed URL, and a CSP `frame-src` entry
  before production.

## Pre-existing security advisor warnings (NOT introduced here)

From the `0001_profiles` migration; flagged for a future hardening pass (relates
to issue #6 / #32), not fixed in the events PR to keep scope clean:

- `set_updated_at` has a mutable `search_path` (set it to `''`/`pg_catalog`).
- `citext` extension installed in `public` schema (move to an `extensions` schema).
- `SECURITY DEFINER` helpers (`is_admin`, `current_user_role`, `handle_new_user`,
  `guard_profile_privileges`, `rls_auto_enable`) are `EXECUTE`-able by
  anon/authenticated via RPC. Low risk (boolean/role helpers) but best practice is
  to `revoke execute ... from anon, authenticated`.

## The deploy fix

Vercel is failing only because **nothing is merged to `main`** — it's building commit `0391380`, which contains a single file (`.gitattributes`). The fix is to merge the stack **#37 → #38 → #39 → #40 → #41** into `main`, in that order. Once `main` has `package.json`, the "No Next.js version detected" error disappears.

## ⚠️ One thing that will bite you right after merge

A green build ≠ a working site. Your pages are all dynamic and read Supabase at **runtime**, so once deployed they'll **500 on every request until you set env vars in Vercel**. The build won't warn you — it passed locally only because `.env.local` exists and no page hits Supabase at build time.

Minimum to set in the Vercel project (Production) before the site works:
- `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL`
- `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`
- `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` (your prod domain — the auth redirects use it)
- `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` (set it now even though MVP paths don't use it yet)

And in **Supabase → Auth → GitHub provider**, add your production `…/auth/callback` to the allowed redirect URLs, or the sign-in funnel dead-ends in prod.

## Your call

Merging to `main` is a production deploy — your guardrail, so I won't do it without a yes. Want me to **merge the whole stack into `main` now** (in order, via `gh`)? Or merge just **#37 baseline** first if you'd rather land the deploy and review the feature PRs separately?

Either way, set those Vercel env vars or the deploy will go green and the live site will still error.

## Environment-Specific Configuration Reference

<!-- Sourced from env-vars skill: Environment-Specific Configuration -->
### Vercel Dashboard vs .env Files

| Use Case | Where to Set |
|----------|-------------|
| Secrets (API keys, tokens) | Vercel Dashboard (`https://vercel.com/{team}/{project}/settings/environment-variables`) or `vercel env add` |
| Public config (site URL, feature flags) | `.env` or `.env.[environment]` files |
| Local-only overrides | `.env.local` |
| CI/CD secrets | Vercel Dashboard (`https://vercel.com/{team}/{project}/settings/environment-variables`) with environment scoping |

### Environment Scoping on Vercel

Variables set in the Vercel Dashboard at `https://vercel.com/{team}/{project}/settings/environment-variables` can be scoped to:

- **Production** — only `vercel.app` production deployments
- **Preview** — branch/PR deployments
- **Development** — `vercel dev` and `vercel env pull`

A variable can be assigned to one, two, or all three environments.

### Git Branch Overrides

Preview environment variables can be scoped to specific Git branches:

```bash
# Add a variable only for the "staging" branch
vercel env add DATABASE_URL preview --git-branch=staging < ./staging-database-url.txt
```

## Common Gotchas

<!-- Sourced from env-vars skill: Gotchas -->
### `vercel env pull` Overwrites Custom Variables

`vercel env pull .env.local` **replaces the entire file** — any manually added variables (custom secrets, local overrides, debug flags) are lost. Always back up or re-add custom vars after pulling:

```bash
# Save custom vars before pulling
grep -v '^#' .env.local | grep -v '^VERCEL_\|^POSTGRES_\|^NEXT_PUBLIC_' > .env.custom.bak
vercel env pull .env.local --yes
cat .env.custom.bak >> .env.local  # Re-append custom vars
```

Or maintain custom vars in a separate `.env.development.local` file (loaded after `.env.local` by Next.js).

### Scripts Don't Auto-Load `.env.local`

Only Next.js auto-loads `.env.local`. Standalone scripts (`drizzle-kit`, `tsx`, custom Node scripts) need explicit loading:

```bash
# Use dotenv-cli
npm install -D dotenv-cli
npx dotenv -e .env.local -- npx drizzle-kit push
npx dotenv -e .env.local -- npx tsx scripts/seed.ts

# Or source manually
source <(grep -v '^#' .env.local | sed 's/^/export /') && node scripts/migrate.js
```

On real-time for the future — you're right that we're not doing it today, but it's a genuinely good fit for a community site down the line. True "who's here now" would use **Supabase Realtime Presence** (clients send heartbeats; you get a live roster) to power things like:

I know we haven't built it yet, but where will the livestream be shown when we do?

Two places, by design — and one of them already has the slot wired up:

## 1. The event's own page (the canonical home of a broadcast)
`app/events/[slug]/page.tsx` **already has the embed slot built.** When an event has `is_live = true` and a `stream_embed_url` set, it renders the Restream player inline at the top of that event's detail page — in a 16:9 frame with the "● Live now" badge — right above the title, description, and RSVP/who's-going. So the full "watch + see who's here + read the details" experience lives on the event page. The columns exist in the schema (migration `0002` added `is_live` + `stream_embed_url`); what's missing is the toggle + the actual Restream URL.

## 2. The home page (the "catch people when they land" surface) — this is #35
This is the original goal you described: *"so that the meetings play on the home page when we're live."* It's **not built yet**, but here's where it'd go now that we have the split hero:

When a broadcast is live, a **"LIVE NOW" bar drops in at the very top of the home page** (above the hero), with the embedded player and a CTA into the event. Roughly:

```
┌─ 🔴 LIVE NOW · Ship-it Thursday ──────── [ Join the stream → ] ┐
│  ┌───────────── embedded Restream player (16:9) ───────────┐  │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  (the normal split hero sits below, or collapses while live)   │
```

When nothing's live, that bar simply isn't rendered and the home page looks exactly as it does now.

Creating my first event.  I see a slug field.  If I am creating a repeating event, how can we handle that, so that the slug is the same each time?

Great question, and it exposes a real design point rather than just a field tip.

**The short answer on slugs:** a slug is **unique per event** — one slug = one event row = one permanent URL. So you *can't* reuse the same slug across multiple separate event rows (the database will reject the duplicate). "Same slug each time" is only possible if a repeating event is modeled as **one recurring thing**, not a new event every week.

And right now, the system only knows about **one-off events** — there's no recurrence concept built yet. So this is a feature decision, not something the slug field alone solves.

**For the event you're creating right this second:** if it's a weekly series (e.g., Ship-it Thursday), give it a **non-dated slug** like `ship-it-thursday` (not `ship-it-thursday-oct-9`). That way, when we add recurrence, this becomes the stable series URL.

Here's the fork for how recurrence should actually work — it affects the schema, RSVPs, and the calendar feed, so I want your call:

options.label: Recurring series (recommended)
options.description: One event + a repeat rule (weekly, etc.). Stable slug/URL that always shows the next occurrence. The iCal feed emits an RRULE so it auto-repeats in subscribers' calendars. RSVPs apply to the series (you're a regular). Simplest, meets 'same slug each time.'

options.label: Series + dated occurrences
options.description: A series (stable slug) with individual dated occurrences underneath — per-occurrence RSVPs, who's-going, and cancellations. Occurrence URLs like /events/ship-it-thursday/2026-10-09. More powerful, bigger build.

options.label: Manual, with a Duplicate button
options.description: No recurrence model. Keep one-off events, but I add a 'Duplicate event' button so you clone next week in one click (it gets a new dated slug each time). Pragmatic stopgap; slug differs per week.

Good catch — "philosopher-s-dinner" would be ugly. The fix is to **strip** apostrophes/quotes before splitting on separators, rather than treating them as dividers. Since the event form's auto-gen and the forum both use the same `slugify`, one fix covers both. Let me update it:

input.new_string:
/**
 * Turn a title into a URL-safe base slug. Apostrophes/quotes and accents are
 * removed (not treated as dividers), so "AI Philosopher's Dinner" becomes
 * "ai-philosophers-dinner", not "ai-philosopher-s-dinner".
 */
export function slugify(input: string): string {
  const base = input
    .normalize("NFKD")
    .replace(/[̀-ͯ]/g, "") // strip combining accent marks (café -> cafe)
    .toLowerCase()
    .replace(/['’‘ʼ`"“”]+/g, "") // drop apostrophes/quotes so they don't become dashes
    .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-") // everything else that isn't alphanumeric -> dash
    .replace(/^-+|-+$/g, "")
    .slice(0, 60)
    .replace(/-+$/g, ""); // tidy a trailing dash left by the slice
  return base || "topic";
}

## My opinion on an end date for recurring events: **yes — but optional and conditional.**

Here's the reasoning:

- **Most of your recurring events are open-ended** ("weekly build stream until we decide to stop"), so the default must be **blank = goes on indefinitely**. Forcing an end date would be annoying for the common case.
- **But bounded series are real and valuable** — a 6-week workshop, a limited cohort, a seasonal thing. Without an end date, you'd have to remember to manually stop it.
- **It matters for the calendar feed specifically.** An infinite `RRULE` means the event sits in subscribers' calendars *forever*, and some clients cap how far they'll expand an endless rule. An end date maps cleanly to `RRULE;UNTIL=…`, so the series cleanly stops in everyone's calendar.

So my recommendation: an **optional "Repeat until" date** that **only appears once you pick a recurrence other than Never** (same conditional pattern as the URL/location fields), blank meaning ongoing.

One alternative worth a mention: instead of an end *date*, some apps use a **count** ("repeat 6 times" → `RRULE;COUNT=6`). I'd go with the **date** — it's more intuitive for "this series runs through December" than counting occurrences. We could even offer both later, but date-only is the right MVP.

Want me to build it? It's small: a `recurrence_until` column, the conditional date field (reusing the picker), and `UNTIL` in the iCal `RRULE`.

**`NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` in your Vercel *Production* environment is set to `http://localhost:3005`.**

Here's why that does it: the sign-in action builds the OAuth callback URL from `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` (`getOrigin()` in `lib/auth/actions.ts`). On prod it's reading `localhost:3005`, so it tells GitHub/Supabase to send users back there.

The Vercel var is the thing redirecting to localhost; the Supabase allow-list is the thing that would reject the *correct* URL once you fix #1 — so do both.

Yes — this is very doable on a free tier, and the key is picking a model that **edits an input photo while keeping the person recognizable**, not one that just generates from text.

## The best free fit: Google's "Nano Banana" (Gemini Flash Image)

This is the standout because it's purpose-built for "keep the subject, restyle everything else" — change outfit/background/pose while the face stays recognizably *them* ([Google's likeness-preservation upgrade](https://tech-now.io/en/blogs/gemini-photo-editor-gemini-2-5-flash-image-the-big-ai-image-editing-leap-august-2025/)), which is exactly "make *me* a comic superhero." It has a usable **free tier through Google AI Studio** — reportedly up to ~500 images/day at 1024², no credit card ([free-tier guide](https://www.aifreeapi.com/en/posts/gemini-image-generation-free-api)). You'd feed it the member's GitHub avatar + a DevsAssemble-branded prompt (halftone, ink outlines, your palette).

Two honest caveats: the exact free limits shift and some sources note image gen is gated/limited on free tiers ([pricing notes](https://curlscape.com/blog/google-gemini-api-pricing-guide-2026)) — verify current quotas; and **Gemini 2.5 Flash Image is slated for deprecation Oct 2026**, so you'd target the current **Gemini 3 Flash Image / Nano Banana** successor.

## The genuinely-free-infrastructure alternative: Cloudflare Workers AI

~10,000 neurons/day free ≈ **~170 FLUX-schnell images/day**, SDXL + FLUX included ([Workers AI free tier](https://www.edenai.co/post/top-free-image-generation-tools-apis-and-open-source-models)). **But these are text-to-image** — they'll make a great *generic* superhero, not one that looks like the member. For likeness you'd need an image-editing model like **FLUX-Kontext** or **InstantID / PhotoMaker / face-to-many**, which are mostly **paid** (Replicate/fal) ([face-preserving models](https://www.edenai.co/post/top-free-image-generation-tools-apis-and-open-source-models)).

## The one thing to decide before building: privacy

You'd be sending **members' faces to a third-party free API**, and free tiers often **train on your inputs** (Google's free tier does). For a likeness feature that's a real consent issue — I'd:
- make it **opt-in** with a clear "your photo is sent to [provider]" notice,
- and if that's a dealbreaker, use a **zero-data-retention paid path** instead (Vercel AI Gateway → Gemini, which has ZDR, is the Vercel-idiomatic option).

## My recommendation

Start with **Nano Banana (Gemini Flash Image) on the AI Studio free tier** — it's the only free option that nails "superhero version of *yourself*," and it's a few-hundred-a-day budget that's plenty for a launching community.

Good question to catch now, because the current behavior is a bit of a trap. Here's exactly what happens today:

- **The image files persist** — each generation uploads to a *new* timestamped path (`<uid>/hero-<timestamp>.png`), never overwriting. So every old superhero PNG is still physically sitting in the `avatars` bucket.
- **But the app only remembers the latest** — `hero_avatar_url` on the profile gets *overwritten* each time. Nothing references the old files.

So the honest answer to "will they have access to the old ones?" is **no** — not through any UI. The old images exist but are effectively orphaned: unreachable unless you happened to save the URL, and they **quietly pile up** in storage forever (same is true for replaced upload photos). That's both a missing feature *and* a slow storage leak.

Two clean ways to resolve it, and I'd like your call:

**Option A — Keep a history (my recommendation).** Show a small "your heroes" gallery on the profile settings page where members can view, **download**, or **re-activate** any past generation. The nice part: we **don't need a new table** — we can just list each member's files from their storage folder (`storage.list(uid)`), so it's low effort and the files we're already keeping become a feature instead of clutter.

**Option B — Keep only the latest.** Delete the previous hero file when a new one is generated (and the old base photo on re-upload). No history, but no orphan buildup.

Given you *just* added "download to use elsewhere," Option A pairs naturally — people can grab any of their past heroes, not just the current one. Want me to build the gallery (A), or go lean and clean up old files (B)?
It's also really important that we do our best to make it look like the person in the photo.

  - **Color accent** (4): blue-led, lime-led, purple-led, or balanced.

Shipped. The **Tools** shelf is live and separate from Projects.

**What you can do now** (on localhost refresh, and on `devsassemble.ai` after this deploys): go to **Tools → Add a tool**, paste `https://entire.io`, pick a category, add a one-line "why it's in your toolbelt," and it's on the shelf — no GitHub repo involved.

**What I built:**
- **New `tools` + `tool_reactions` tables** (migration `0010`, applied to Supabase). RLS mirrors Projects: public read, signed-in users submit their own, author/admin edit/delete. Security advisor confirms no RLS gaps.
- **`/tools` page** — grid of tool cards with **category filter chips** (All · AI · DevOps · Design · Productivity · Other) plus **Newest / Most loved** sort, exactly like Projects.
- **Tool cards** show the site's favicon, category badge, the tool name linking out, the domain, your "why" note, who shared it, and the same 👍🔥🤯⭐ reactions.
- **`/tools/new`** submit form: name, URL, category chips, optional note. URLs are normalized and de-duped.
- **"Tools"** added to the public and app nav headers.

**The clean split, as you framed it:**
- **Projects** = things *built* — GitHub repos, with stars/language/Discuss.
- **Tools** = things *useful* — any URL, no repo required.

A couple of optional follow-ups I deliberately left out to keep scope tight — say the word and I'll add any:
- Surface new tools in the **home activity feed** (currently only events/discussions/projects feed it).
- Let members **edit/delete their own tools** from a profile or the card (RLS already allows it; there's just no UI yet — same gap Projects has).
- Auto-fetch the tool's **page title** to pre-fill the name field.

content.text:
Done and pushed. Signed-in users now get the **authenticated nav everywhere**.

**What changed:**
- **`PublicHeader`** (used by events, projects, tools, discussions, profiles) now renders `AppHeader` when a user is signed in — so you get the full nav (Projects · Tools · Discussions · Events), the Admin link if you're staff, your username, and Sign out — instead of the generic "Sign in" CTA.
- **The home page** does the same: logged-in users see `AppHeader`; logged-out visitors keep the marketing header with its on-page anchors (How it works / Events / Community) and the "Sign in" button.
- **`AppHeader` is now sticky** with the same cream backdrop as the public header, so the nav stays visible on scroll — a small consistency win for the app shell (dashboard/settings/admin) too.

One source of truth for the authenticated nav, so adding a nav item in `AppHeader` now updates it for logged-in users across the whole site. The mobile menu still works since `AppHeader`'s `sticky` provides the positioning context its dropdown anchors to.
